hints: Notice the question asks for amplitude $A$, not intensity, and gives the angle $\theta$ between the incident plane of polarisation and the filter transmission axis.
Recall that only the vector component of oscillation parallel to the transmission axis passes through, so resolve $A$ into parallel and perpendicular components.
Compare $\cos\theta$ for amplitude with $\cos^2\theta$ for intensity, and check that an amplitude answer must still have the same units as $A$.
walkthrough: Identify the given information: incident plane polarised wave of amplitude $A$ meets the filter with its vibration direction at angle $\theta$ to the transmission axis.
State the physical rule: the filter transmits only the component of the wave displacement parallel to its transmission axis and absorbs the perpendicular component.
Set up the vector resolution: parallel component $= A\cos\theta$ and perpendicular component $= A\sin\theta$.
Note the distinction from Malus law for intensity: since intensity is proportional to (amplitude)$^2$, intensity follows $I = I_0\cos^2\theta$, but amplitude follows the first power of cosine.
Reject options with $A^2$ because amplitude must have the same dimension as $A$, not $A^2$.
Therefore the emerging amplitude is $A\cos\theta$. This is option A.

options.A: The component of displacement along the transmission axis is $A\cos\theta$, so this amplitude is transmitted.
options.B: $A\cos^2\theta$ confuses amplitude with intensity - intensity is proportional to amplitude squared and follows $\cos^2\theta$.
options.C: $A^2\cos\theta$ is impossible for amplitude because $A^2$ has units of (displacement)$^2$, which relates to intensity not amplitude.
options.D: $A^2\cos^2\theta$ describes how intensity varies, not the transmitted displacement amplitude.
